input: A completed TypeScript change contains two identical private helpers, one unused import, and a loop that manually performs a supported Array method. The focused tests pass.
expect: The agent runs the focused tests first, removes the unused import, merges the repeated helper logic, uses the supported clear native method, then runs the same tests and relevant formatter and static checks. The report names structural reductions rather than only a line count.

input: A named Rust scope has a private helper called parse_customer_policy that is called once. Inlining it saves five lines but hides the domain operation inside a long match expression.
expect: The agent keeps the helper because its name preserves a domain concept and inlining harms readability. The report lists it under Kept. No line-count target overrides that decision.

input: The target tests fail before any simplify edit because the fixture cannot connect to its test database.
expect: The agent stops without editing code and reports the exact baseline command and failure. It does not infer that the proposed reductions are safe and does not run an after result as if it were comparable.

input: A request handler checks that a decoded JSON field is present, although the internal typed object marks the field as required. External clients can still omit the field before decoding.
expect: The agent keeps the runtime boundary check because untyped external data enters there. It does not treat the internal required type as proof about external input.

input: A Python module has a function with no textual callers. The framework loads handlers from a configuration string, and the function name appears in that configuration.
expect: The agent searches configured and reflective uses before removal, finds the string entry point, and keeps the function. It does not equate no textual caller with dead code.

input: A JavaScript patch can shrink from twelve lines to four by joining statements with semicolons, using one-letter names, and nesting three conditional expressions. Tests would still pass.
expect: The agent rejects the rewrite as code golf. It does not claim formatting, packed statements, or short names as simplification, and it preserves the readable form.

input: Simplify the implementation changed by this task. The task diff edits a shared function used across several modules and changes behavior at an interface boundary. Review the code and make the smallest safe simplification.
expect: The response must inspect every module affected by the change, including callers, callees, side effects across call paths, and behavior at module or interface boundaries. It must not limit review scope to files or lines in the task diff. It must identify affected modules before proposing or applying a simplification and preserve their observed behavior. Fail responses that review only the task diff, even if the local edit is valid.

input: A changed TypeScript request handler has deeply nested checks. Guard clauses preserve behavior, make each rejection direct, and lower its measured complexity. The focused tests pass.
expect: The agent runs `rust-code-analysis-cli --metrics --output-format json --paths <file>` before the edit. It walks the JSON spaces tree to find the function record. It reduces the nested control flow because clarity improves. It runs the same command again and reports both function metrics with the focused test result. It does not add a helper only to lower the metric.

input: A changed TypeScript function has twelve flat match cases. The analyzer reports a cyclomatic-complexity score of 12. Each case is short, direct, and maps one protocol value to one result. Extracting helpers would only hide the cases. The focused tests pass.
expect: The agent reports the rust-code-analysis-cli function record as a review signal and keeps the flat match. It explains that the score stays high because the direct branches are clearer. It does not extract helpers or claim that a lower score is always better.

input: Assess this proposed simplification, not a live edit. JavaScript: function count(rows) { let total = 0; for (const row of rows) { for (let slot = 0; slot < 4; slot++) { total += row[slot]; } } return total; } Each row has exactly four numbers; rows has n entries. A proposal replaces the loops with rows.flat().reduce((sum, value) => sum + value, 0). Give a concrete keep/change decision, runtime and peak storage for both, and derive them. Do not run tests or claim edits on this paper-only comparison.
expect: Keeps the direct bounded loop unless a concrete readability reason outweighs the allocation. Original performs 4n additions: Theta(n) runtime, Theta(1) auxiliary and scalar output. flat creates 4n entries before reduce: Theta(n) runtime and Theta(n) auxiliary, scalar output. Rejects an alleged quadratic original based on syntax. Does not invent benchmark or test results. Generic advice without solving the example scores at most 2.

input: Assess this JavaScript simplification on paper: original unique(items) uses an initially empty Set and result array, loops over items, and pushes x only when !seen.has(x), then seen.add(x). Proposed: function unique(items) { return items.filter((x, index) => items.indexOf(x) === index); } Inputs are n finite integers; preserve first occurrence order. Give before/after runtime and output versus auxiliary storage, a worst-case input, and whether to accept the change. Assume expected constant-time Set operations.
expect: Rejects proposed regression. Distinct input makes indexOf visit 1+2+...+n entries, Theta(n^2) versus expected Theta(n) original. Output has k unique entries, Theta(k) both; original Set adds Theta(k) auxiliary, proposal Theta(1) auxiliary excluding filter output. Notes the explicit expected hash assumption, not an unconditional worst-case linear claim. Explains actual library scans; simply saying use a Set is insufficient.

input: Assess this implementation without editing files: function pairs(left, right) { const result = []; for (const a of left) for (const b of right) result.push([a, b]); return result; } left has n entries, right m independently; both may grow. Contract requires the complete ordered array of pairs. A suggestion says replace result with a generator to obtain constant memory and calls the old code quadratic. Decide and derive runtime, returned storage and auxiliary storage with the dimensions named.
expect: For positive n,m derives nm pair writes: Theta(nm) time, Theta(nm) returned storage, Theta(1) auxiliary excluding output. Does not assume n=m; for empty sides may use O(n+nm) for this literal loop. Rejects generator as a contract change, and explains required materialized output imposes the storage cost. No unsupported claim that this is removable quadratic auxiliary memory.

input: Review a proposed simplification on paper. function collect(keys, store) { const result = []; for (const key of keys) result.push(store.lookup(key)); return result; } keys has n entries. store.lookup implementation and cost contract are unavailable. Each returned value is one scalar; calls may have side effects. A proposal batches or caches calls to claim linear time. What can you establish, what is missing, and should the proposal ship?
expect: Derives n calls plus array work: O(n + sum_i T_lookup(i)); Theta(n) returned references, O(1) local auxiliary apart from callee memory and array growth. States total peak auxiliary needs callee allocation/lifetime evidence. Does not invent constant lookup or quadratic total. Requests lookup implementation/contract and side-effect/order evidence before batching or caching. Does not replace fixture analysis with repeated policy text.

input: Assess a shorter JavaScript replacement on paper. Original: function sum(values) { let result = 0; for (const value of values) result += value; return result; } Proposed: function sum(values) { return values.reduce((state, value) => ({ history: [...state.history, value], total: state.total + value }), { history: [], total: 0 }).total; } n finite integers, arithmetic and allocation proportional to array length. What changed in runtime and peak live memory? Would you keep it?
expect: Rejects unnecessary history. Spread copies prefix lengths 0 through n-1, Theta(n^2) total work/allocation versus Theta(n) time before. Peak live auxiliary is Theta(n), not Theta(n^2), under reclaimable unreachable arrays; cumulative allocation is quadratic. Scalar result and original Theta(1) auxiliary distinguished. Explains the spread work rather than counting visible loops.

input: Assess this code for simplification without editing files. function countCommon(a, b) { let i = 0, j = 0, count = 0; while (i < a.length) { while (j < b.length && b[j] < a[i]) j++; if (j < b.length && b[j] === a[i]) count++; i++; } return count; } a and b are sorted arrays of distinct finite integers with independent lengths n,m. Is replacing it with a.filter(x => b.includes(x)).length a safe simplification in cost? Derive both, including memory.
expect: Keeps the two-pointer scan: i advances at most n times and j never resets, advances at most m, so O(n+m) time and O(1) auxiliary. Proposed includes does up to m comparisons per a element, worst-case Theta(nm), with Theta(k) temporary filtered entries where k matches; scalar output. Does not label existing nesting quadratic or collapse independent sizes without stating n=m. Recognizes unchanged code is justified.
